story_ideas.title: CMS refreshed dataset: Ownership
story_ideas.headline: You can look up who owns your parent's nursing home, and what else they own
story_ideas.angle: A walkthrough of the Ownership file refreshed 08/01/26, joined to Facility Affiliation Data, for families comparing two or three homes in one county.
story_ideas.hook: The file names the parties behind a facility, which turns a single-building decision into a portfolio question.
story_ideas.consumer: Before you tour a home, pull its ownership record and check what else the same owners operate near you, then look up those buildings too.
story_ideas.b2b: Chain operators should expect ownership joins to become the default frame for facility-level coverage, and should know what their own affiliation record currently says.
story_ideas.why: Families who look only at the building in front of them miss a pattern that the public record already contains.
story_ideas.note: Breaks to states and counties; no monitored publisher matched it, and it charts cleanly as facilities per owner.

story_ideas.title: CMS refreshed dataset: Penalties
story_ideas.headline: The fines your nursing home paid are public again
story_ideas.angle: A plain-language guide to the Penalties file refreshed 08/01/26 for adult children who have never opened a CMS download.
story_ideas.hook: Civil money penalties and payment denials are itemized per facility and refreshed monthly, and almost nobody reads them before signing an admission agreement.
story_ideas.consumer: Ask the admissions director about any penalty listed against the facility, and bring the record with you rather than relying on the answer alone.
story_ideas.b2b: Providers should assume a fine now travels with the building in every state comparison a reporter runs.
story_ideas.why: A penalty history you never see is one you cannot ask about while you still have a choice.
story_ideas.note: State and county level; strong candidate for a state-by-state ranking.

story_ideas.title: CMS refreshed dataset: Health Deficiencies
story_ideas.headline: What inspectors actually wrote about the home you are touring
story_ideas.angle: Reading the Health Deficiencies file refreshed 08/01/26 alongside the Citation Code Look-up so a family can decode a citation instead of skipping it.
story_ideas.hook: The citations exist in public, in code, and the look-up table that translates them refreshed on the same day.
story_ideas.consumer: Match each citation code against the look-up file so you know whether the finding was about paperwork or about resident harm.
story_ideas.b2b: Survey teams can anticipate which citation categories will get consumer-facing translation this cycle.
story_ideas.why: Knowing what a deficiency actually described is the difference between ruling a home out and asking a better question.

story_ideas.title: CMS refreshed dataset: Fire Safety Deficiencies
story_ideas.headline: The safety inspection nobody asks about on the tour
story_ideas.angle: The Fire Safety Deficiencies file refreshed 08/01/26, treated as the one record families never think to check.
story_ideas.hook: Fire safety findings are tracked separately from health deficiencies, so a facility can look clean on one and not the other.
story_ideas.consumer: Check the fire safety record separately from the health inspection record, because a home can pass one and be cited on the other.
story_ideas.b2b: Life safety code findings are an underused differentiator for operators who clear them consistently.
story_ideas.why: You can rule out a building on a record you did not know was published.
story_ideas.note: State and county detail supports a map.

story_ideas.title: CMS refreshed dataset: Hospice care - State CAHPS Hospice Survey Data
story_ideas.headline: How families in your state rate hospice care
story_ideas.angle: State-level CAHPS Hospice Survey results refreshed 08/07/26, compared across states for readers arranging end-of-life care.
story_ideas.hook: The survey captures bereaved families' assessments and is published at the state level, so ranking is immediate.
story_ideas.consumer: Compare your state's hospice survey results against neighboring states before you agree to the first agency a hospital suggests.
story_ideas.b2b: Hospice providers face a public state benchmark that boards and referral partners can read without help.
story_ideas.why: Choosing a hospice on a hospital's referral alone means ignoring the only systematic account of what other families experienced.
story_ideas.note: Pairs with the national CAHPS file refreshed the same day; no monitored publisher matched either.

story_ideas.title: Medicaid Home and Community-Based Services for Older Adults: A Primer
story_ideas.headline: The care most people want is the hardest to research
story_ideas.angle: Justice in Aging's 08/20/26 primer on Medicaid home and community-based services, read as a guide for families weighing home care against a facility.
story_ideas.hook: HCBS is the alternative to institutional care and has no facility-level penalty or inspection file to compare against.
story_ideas.consumer: Find out what your state's Medicaid program covers at home before assuming a nursing home is the only route.

trends_raw: This run carried 170 evidence candidates against 169 in the run dated 09/04/26, with nothing first surfacing today. Medicare and Medicaid and long-term care each gained an item; fraud and scams, financial security and housing each lost one. Medicare and Medicaid remains the busiest beat at 27 items from seven sources, but it does not cohere at 0.052, so those items share a tag and nothing else and should be worked as separate leads rather than a single story. The same caution applies to housing at 0.028, caregiving at 0.034, workforce at 0.084 and financial security at 0.089. Three clusters do hold: palliative and hospice care is the tightest in the run at 0.457, with nine items from CMS provider data and RAND and none matched by monitored publishers; long-term care holds at 0.257 across 18 items; depression and mental health holds at 0.112 across three. The run's shape is a file-heavy month, dominated by the 07/31/26 to 08/11/26 CMS provider refresh, which is why the reporting value sits in joining files rather than in any single one. Coverage posture: 82 confirmed gaps, plus 78 items on beats where we watch no publisher at all, which is a limit on what we can see and not a claim that nobody has written them.
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Fifteen of the CMS provider files that sit underneath a nursing home's public profile refreshed between 07/31/26 and 08/11/26 — Ownership, Facility Affiliation Data, Penalties, Health Deficiencies, Fire Safety Deficiencies, Survey Summary, Inspection Dates, MDS Quality Measures and the Citation Code Look-up among them. Refreshed together, they stop being separate downloads and become one joinable record: a facility can be traced to its owners, its owners to their other facilities, and each facility to what it was cited and fined for, with the code look-up translating the citation numbers into plain language. Justice in Aging's Medicaid Home and Community-Based Services primer (08/20/26) describes the alternative most families weigh against a facility, and the Center for Retirement Research's comparison of long-term care in Israel and the United States (09/03/26) sets both against another country's system. All three sit in one cluster that holds together at 0.257 cohesion.

**Why it matters:** A family choosing a nursing home this month can now check whether the chain behind it has been fined elsewhere, not just whether this building has. That capability is limited to institutional care. The home and community-based side, which the 08/20/26 primer covers, carries no equivalent facility-level file of penalties and inspections, so the option many older adults prefer is also the one they can research least. Sixteen of the 18 items in this cluster went unmatched by the publishers we monitor, and 15 break below the national level to state and county, so the comparison can be made concrete anywhere.

**Why pitch this now:** The deficiency, penalty and inspection files carry an August 2026 stamp and will be overwritten at the next refresh, so the version a story is built on is the version families are looking at right now. The Federal Register's IPPS and long-term care hospital payment document published 08/04/26 sits in the same window, and the Center for Retirement Research piece landed 09/03/26.

**Angle:** Whether the public record families rely on to judge a nursing home is complete enough to answer the question they are actually asking, which is not how this building scores but who runs it and what else they run. Working title: "The Owner Behind the Rating." For operators and compliance staff who know these files exist, and for the adult children who do not.

**Potential headlines:**
- The fines your nursing home paid are public again
- One company, twelve buildings, and a citation record you can now follow
- The care option with no inspection file

**Potential outlets:**
- **McKnight's Long-Term Care News** — its readers are the survey and compliance staff who live inside the deficiency and citation files, and it can carry the argument that ownership joins change what a facility's record shows.
- **Skilled Nursing News** — covers chain finance and M&A, which is exactly what Ownership and Facility Affiliation Data together make traceable across a portfolio.
- **Family Caregiver Alliance** — reaches families mid-decision, the audience for a walkthrough of what the penalty and inspection records actually say about a building.
- **Kiplinger** — pairs the institutional record with the Medicaid HCBS primer for readers weighing what long-term care will cost them and where.

**You can look up who owns your parent's nursing home, and what else they own**
*CMS refreshed dataset: Ownership*  
- Angle: A walkthrough of the Ownership file refreshed 08/01/26, joined to Facility Affiliation Data, for families comparing two or three homes in one county.
- Hook: The file names the parties behind a facility, which turns a single-building decision into a portfolio question.
- For readers: Before you tour a home, pull its ownership record and check what else the same owners operate near you, then look up those buildings too.
- For the trade: Chain operators should expect ownership joins to become the default frame for facility-level coverage, and should know what their own affiliation record currently says.
- Why it matters: Families who look only at the building in front of them miss a pattern that the public record already contains.
- Also: Breaks to states and counties; no monitored publisher matched it, and it charts cleanly as facilities per owner.
